title: Where Will Maxi Look for the Chocolate?
text:
At the University of Salzburg in Austria, Heinz Wimmer and Josef Perner wanted to know when children begin to understand that other people can believe something that is not true. They designed a short story acted out with toys.

A boy named Maxi helps his mother unpack the shopping and puts some chocolate in a blue cupboard. Then he goes out to play. While he is away, his mother takes the chocolate out, uses some for a cake, and puts the rest in a green cupboard. Maxi comes back, hungry for chocolate. The child listening to the story was asked a simple question: where will Maxi look for the chocolate?

The child knew where the chocolate really was. To answer correctly, they had to set aside their own knowledge and reason from Maxi's point of view: he did not see it moved, so he will look in the blue cupboard. The youngest children, around three and four, mostly pointed to the green cupboard, where the chocolate actually was. Between about four and six, more and more children gave the right answer, and most older children found it easy.

The false belief test became one of the most widely used tools in developmental psychology and in research on autism.
lesson: Understanding that others see the world differently from us is learned, not given. Help children practice it by asking what someone else knows and feels.
source: Wimmer, H., and Perner, J. (1983). Beliefs about beliefs: Representation and constraining function of wrong beliefs in young children's understanding of deception. Cognition, 13(1), 103-128.
caveat: Some later studies using nonverbal methods suggest that infants may grasp false beliefs earlier than verbal tests show, though these results have been hard to replicate.
